title: Flood response and SPD voting in Germany
table: Table 1, column 3, expressed as a first-difference regression
unit: Electoral district; one row for its 1998-to-2002 change

original_reference.notes: Original two-period model: 299 district effects, a period effect, ten time-varying controls, and district-clustered standard errors. The source panel contains 598 rows. First differencing gives the supplied 299-row dataset and preserves the original coefficient and standard error when the original finite-sample correction is applied.

sample_notes: All 299 districts have two complete source rows; no observations are dropped, imputed, or reweighted. There are 29 flooded districts.
The supplied regression includes an intercept. First differencing removes district effects; the intercept captures the common election-period change. No panel estimator is needed.

The authors' original harmonized district boundaries and stored covariate scales are preserved. Covariate values belong to the source election rows; the source appendix describes their measurement dates only as selected years.

The original regression contains exactly ten control changes. The additional covariate columns retain the source values for the two election rows and are excluded from this regression. District IDs identify observations and do not enter the regression.

The first-difference regression reproduces the original coefficient and standard error. Multiply its HC0 covariance by G/(G-1) * (2G-1)/(2G-q-1), where G=299 districts and q=12 coefficients including the intercept, exposure and ten control changes. Use t inference with 298 degrees of freedom.

Published source: Bechtel and Hainmueller (2011), How Lasting Is Voter Gratitude? An Analysis of the Short- and Long-term Electoral Returns to Beneficial Policy, American Journal of Political Science, DOI 10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00533.x.
identification_notes: This remains a comparison of changes in flooded and unaffected districts. A causal interpretation requires an appropriate parallel-trends assumption.
Some time-varying controls could themselves respond to the flood. The original covariate-adjusted specification does not resolve this concern or separately identify the effect of relief spending.
The original standard-error convention does not address spatial correlation between neighboring districts. Flood exposure is geographically concentrated.
